title: Match on Numbers
story: You need to convert digits to words: 1 becomes 'one,' 2 becomes 'two.' A match statement reads like a dictionary — every number gets its word, and the catch-all handles anything beyond your list.
why: Matching on literal numbers is the simplest and most readable way to map values to outcomes — cleaner than if-else chains for discrete values.
analogy: Matching on numbers is like a restaurant menu — item #1 is 'Burger,' #2 is 'Pizza.' You don't need to explain the logic; the mapping IS the documentation.
try_it: Extend `number_name` to count to 20. Then write `roman_numeral(n: Int) -> Str` that converts 1-10 to Roman numerals (I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, X). Use match on exact numbers. Test edge cases: 0 and 11.
tips: Literal patterns match exact values — `1 =>` only matches when the value is exactly 1
Multiple values can share the same outcome by writing separate arms with the same body
Always include a `_ =>` catch-all for values outside your expected range
common_mistakes: Using ranges in literal patterns — `1..5 =>` is not valid (that's what guards are for)
Writing `1, 2, 3 => "something"` thinking it creates a list pattern — use separate arms or guards
Forgetting that match order matters — a catch-all `_` before specific literal arms eats all matches
